title: Leveraging AI-Mediated Information Environment for Democracy
intro: AI systems have become central intermediaries in modern democracy. Social media algorithms curate what political content people see and whom they connect with, large language models retrieve and interpret political information, and public institutions increasingly use AI to communicate with their constituents.

This shift introduces a fundamental tension. Commercial platforms optimize AI systems for engagement, time-on-platform, and revenue, goals that often favor sensational, polarizing, or emotionally charged content. Democracy, by contrast, needs information environments that value accuracy, expose people to diverse perspectives, and support informed decision-making.
question: How can AI-mediated information systems better support democratic processes?
outline: My dissertation consists of three empirical studies, each examining a different dimension of the information environment that AI systems can either distort or enhance.

chapters.question: Can reducing exposure to untrustworthy sources durably reduce engagement with them?
chapters.title: Muting Durably Reduces Engagement with Untrustworthy Online Sources; Media Literacy Doesn't
chapters.authors: Do Won Kim, Brendan Nyhan, Ro'ee Levy, Filippo Menczer, Maria Elizabeth (Betsi) Grabe, Giovanni Luca Ciampaglia
chapters.status: Dissertation Chapter 1: field experiment on X (Twitter)
chapters.summary: A digital field experiment comparing muting untrustworthy accounts with a media literacy intervention. Muting produced substantial, lasting reductions in engagement with targeted sources with no compensatory shift elsewhere; media literacy only temporarily improved discernment without changing behavior.

chapters.question: Can conversations with an AI that unexpectedly agrees across party lines, or disagrees within them, correct distorted views of partisans and reduce polarization?
chapters.title: Challenging Partisan Expectations Reduces Political Polarization
chapters.authors: Do Won Kim, Ozgur Can Seckin, Saumya Bhadani, Alessandro Flammini, Giovanni Luca Ciampaglia, Bao Tran Truong
chapters.status: Dissertation Chapter 2: survey experiment with LLM chatbots
chapters.summary: A 2x2 survey experiment varying an LLM chatbot's partisan identity and conversational stance. Ingroup disagreement and outgroup agreement both reduced polarization by updating perceptions of group diversity and extremity, not by persuading participants on policy views.

chapters.question: Can a civic AI chatbot improve access to official election information, and in turn, knowledge of voting procedures and trust in elections?
chapters.title: Can AI Strengthen Democracy? Improving Public Trust in Elections with a Civic Chatbot
chapters.authors: Do Won Kim, Giovanni Luca Ciampaglia, Cody Buntain, Riley Lankes, Patrick Wu
chapters.status: Dissertation Chapter 3: planned 3-arm RCT, Nov. 2026 midterms, Montgomery County, MD
chapters.summary: A randomized experiment testing whether a RAG chatbot that answers only from official election information improves voter knowledge, trust in election administration, and civic engagement.
